author: Annette Cary
title: Fusion energy developer plans to manufacture in Tri-Cities, create 100s of jobs - NewsBreak
text:
By Annette Cary ,
6 hours ago Robin Langtry, co-founder & CEO of Avalanche Energy, left, and Karl Dye, President & CEO of TRIDEC, sign an agreement Thursday afternoon during a press conference to announce Avalanche's plans for a fusion machine manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities. Dignitaries, including Congressman Dan Newhouse, wearing brown jacket, and Gov. Bob Ferguson stand behind them. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com A company developing technology for compact fusion energy machines announced plans Thursday to manufacture them in the Tri-Cities area, potentially creating hundreds of permanent jobs in the long term.
Avalanche Energy Designs and the Tri-City Development Council signed a letter Thursday outlining their intent to work together to select a site for Avalanche’s first plant, work on needed permits, prepare infrastructure, develop a regional supply chain and develop the specialized skilled workforce that will be needed.
The costs of developing and constructing the proposed manufacturing plant is estimated to be close to $1 billion to be paid for with private funds.
Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson , who spoke at the TRIDEC announcement in Kennewick, called the planned manufacturing center a “big deal,” saying it would be significant for the state’s clean energy future, its climate goals, its manufacturing economy and jobs.
The state already has one of the strongest concentrations of fusion companies and talent anywhere in the world, and Avalanche’s announcement that it planned to build a manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities area further establishes Washington state as a global leader in fusion, he said.
Robin Langtry, co-founder & CEO of Avalanche Energy, left, and Karl Dye, President & CEO of TRIDEC, sign an agreement Thursday afternoon during a press conference to announce Avalanche's plans for a fusion machine manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities. Dignitaries, including Congressman Dan Newhouse, wearing brown jacket, and Gov. Bob Ferguson stand behind them. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com Fusion manufacturing also would further establish the Tri-Cities as a global leader in energy innovation, and at the same time it would bring added prosperity to the region, said Rep. Dan Newhouse, R-Wash. , who also spoke at the announcement.
The project would bring construction jobs initially that would also help the support services industry and then hundreds of skilled and unskilled jobs, he said. It also would attract new investment to the region, he predicted.
Initially, Avalanche plans a prototype production facility that would transition into a commercial manufacturing operation, according to a TRIDEC announcement.
“We envision a world-class manufacturing center that can produce hundreds of fusion machines each year,” said Robin Langtry, chief executive officer of Avalanche Energy.
Fusion technology development Unlike nuclear fission, which splits atoms to release energy, as is done in nuclear power reactors, nuclear fusion is based on a concept of fusing atoms together to release energy.
But there is still work to be done on the technology.
There is no commercial fusion energy production industry yet, as development continues among fusion companies to produce more energy from a fusion reaction than it takes to create the reaction.
Robin Langtry, co-founder & CEO of Avalanche Energy, answers media questions prior to Thursday's press conference to announce his company’s plans for a fusion machine manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com Avalanche, a Seattle-based startup, is on track to demonstrate net fusion energy gain before 2030, it said.
It plans to also be ready to start construction on a prototype plant by then.
Avalanche already has made major breakthroughs in plasma physics and on the machine it is developing in the last five years, including most recently reaching a plasma temperature of 20 million degrees Fahrenheit, or the temperature of the surface of the sun, it said.
A fusion reaction that produces more energy that it requires, relies on a high temperature, a confined space and time for molecules to interact and fuse.
Avalanche already in Tri-Cities Avalanche plans to eventually manufacture a 5-megawatt machine for a system that can fit in a shipping container. It would be small enough to deploy to remote and isolated environments, with possible uses for data centers, disaster relief and defense.
“The Tri-Cities has been an exceptional partner in Avalanche’s journey from an emerging fusion technology company to a company preparing for commercial-scale manufacturing,” Langtry said.
A mock-up of the fusion machine is displayed during Thursday's press conference to announce Avalanche's plans for a fusion machine manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com “We came (to the Tri-Cities) looking for a facility, but what we actually found was a community that really cares about advanced nuclear and a workforce that has a lot of the experience to operate these machines,” he said.
Avalanche already has a presence in the Tri-Cities , with FusionWERX, which was launched in spring 2025. It is a research and development facility in 20,300 square feet of office, warehouse and cleanroom space owned by the Port of Benton at 2345 Stevens Drive in Richland.
FusionWERX is a first-of-its-kind commercial-scale testing facility for advanced fusion technologies, offering access to private companies, universities, national laboratories and others working to accelerate the path to commercial fusion power.
It was launched to speed the transition of fusion from the lab to the real world.
Avalanche needed the FusionWERX space to advance from creating fusion with interactions between molecules of deuterium to interactions between deuterium and tritium, which is radioactive, to take its development to the next step.
The tritium is consumed in the reaction, creating no radioactive waste.
Not only does Avalanche need to develop a process that creates more energy than it uses, but it also needs to investigate materials that can withstand the high heat of its fusion machine, an issue that FusionWERX can help resolve.
The proposed manufacturing facility would operate near FusionWERX.
What Tri-Cities offers Avalanche A fusion energy machine company would be the next step for a community steeped in nuclear history after its workers made nearly two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear weapons program from World War II through the Cold War. It then developed non-defense nuclear projects, from the Fast Flux Test Facility research reactor to the Pacific Northwest’s only commercial nuclear power plant to Energy Northwest’s planned Cascade Advanced Energy Facility , a small modular nuclear reactor.
The Avalanche plant is the next step to build on the Tri-Cities reputation as a nuclear energy hub and also its position as the only place in the Northwest with nearby nuclear, hydro, wind and solar production, said Karl Dye, TRIDEC president.
“The success of FusionWERX demonstrated that this community has the talent, infrastructure, technical expertise and collaborative spirit required to advance breakthrough energy technologies,” Langtry said. “Establishing our first global manufacturing facility here is the natural next step.”
Robin Langtry, co-founder & CEO of Avalanche Energy, during a press conference to announce Avalanche's plans for a fusion machine manufacturing facility in the Tri-Cities. Bob Brawdy/bbrawdy@tricityherald.com It will draw on the Tri-Cities’ experienced nuclear and advanced manufacturing workforce, including scientists, engineers, technicians, fabricators and radiation safety professionals. In addition, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Washington State University Tri-Cities, both in Richland, can offer research expertise.
It also has rail, highway and barge availability to provide access to regional, national and international markets, said TRIDEC.
TRIDEC will coordinate identification of the location for the manufacturing plant.
It intends to issue a request for information to its economic development partners to evaluate potential sites based on the project’s infrastructure, workforce, transportation, utility and development requirements.
Avalanche could start fairly small with a plant that requires about 20 acres of land, but expansion could eventually require hundreds of acres.
“We believe the Tri-Cities can become much more than the place where Avalanche manufactures its fusion machines,” Langtry said. “It can become a place where the next generation of fusion technology is researched, engineered, built and ultimately deployed around the world.”
